summary: Gives authors of Reliable Multicast Transport building block and protocol definitions guidelines so their documents fully explain operation and use. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3269 tells authors what to explain when they document reliable multicast components and protocols. Its checklists help readers understand how components fit together, where they work, and what limits apply.

questions: how to write rmt protocol specifications
what should an rmt building block document include
subtitle: A guide to the information authors should include in reliable multicast specifications.

tldr.problem: Reliable Multicast Transport documents describe reusable building blocks and complete protocol designs, but authors need to explain their limits and dependencies so the parts can be combined safely.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives checklists for building-block documents and for protocol-instantiation documents, covering use, interfaces, dependencies, architecture, behavior, packets, and security.
tldr.outcome: The guidelines help readers understand how an RMT component is intended to work and how a complete protocol combines components. This Informational RFC does not define an RMT protocol.

today: RFC 3269 is an Informational RFC published in May 2002. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why RMT Uses Reusable Components
sections.content:
Reliable Multicast Transport (RMT) can be built in different ways because applications have different requirements. The RFC describes a modular approach: reusable building blocks provide functions that can be combined into protocol instantiations.

A building block needs a clear account of what it does, how it interacts with other blocks, and where it fits in the complete design. Without that information, blocks that work in pairs may fail when combined, or a block may be used outside the conditions it supports.
sections.plainLanguage: RMT protocols can combine reusable components in different ways. Authors need to explain each component's limits and dependencies so readers can tell whether a combination will work.

sections.title: What a Building-Block Document Explains
sections.content:
A building-block document MUST explain why the block exists and why its chosen size is useful. It MUST describe its functions and external interfaces so other components can use it.

Its applicability statement MUST identify intended scenarios, known failure modes and how to detect them, relevant environments, and possible conflicts with other blocks. The document must also describe required packet-header information or abstract messages, list requirements placed on other blocks, and address special security issues when they apply.
sections.plainLanguage: A component's document must say what it does, how other components connect to it, and when it is suitable. It must also list failures, dependencies, and any special security issues.

sections.title: What a Protocol-Instantiation Document Explains
sections.content:
A protocol-instantiation document explains how to combine building blocks into a working protocol. Its applicability statement identifies the applications, scale, environments, and known weaknesses the protocol is intended to address.

The architecture section lists the blocks and how they connect. The document also provides complete algorithms, an application interface, and exact packet formats for IPv4 and IPv6, including IPsec support. It MUST include the conformance statement specified by the RFC, referring to the requirements in RFC 2357.
sections.plainLanguage: A complete protocol document must show how its components work together and what the protocol is for. It must give enough detail about algorithms and messages for readers to understand the whole design.

sections.title: Security and Extensible Choices
sections.content:
The completed protocol-instantiation document has the main responsibility for security requirements, in line with RFC 2357. A building-block document MUST still address special security issues caused by its communications or intended use.

Some blocks define a general framework but leave the choice of algorithm to an implementation. In that case, the document must explain codepoint considerations, including how specific algorithms or options can be identified and extended.
sections.plainLanguage: The complete protocol document must discuss security. A component must also describe unusual security risks it creates and explain how implementations identify choices that the component leaves open.

sections.title: Using the Author Checklists
sections.content:
RFC 3269 ends its two sets of guidelines with checklists. One checklist covers building blocks, including rationale, functions, applicability, packet information, dependencies, and security. The other covers complete protocol instantiations, including applicability, architecture, conformance, functionality, and packet formats.

The RFC says its guidelines supplement common Internet specification-writing practice. It has no explicit IANA considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: The two checklists help authors check that their documents cover the required topics. They supplement the usual practices for writing Internet specifications.
